title: Controllable First-Frame-Guided Video Editing via Mask-Aware LoRA Fine-Tuning
claim: One method turns a source video into a coherent edit from a first-frame reference, with optional extra reference frames for finer temporal control.
layout: 3 stacked filmstrip rows, top-to-bottom, curved arrows linking source frames to edits
description: Three horizontal filmstrip rows, each with three video frames, are stacked vertically. The top row is the source video: a white hibiscus flower blooming against a teal background. The middle row is labeled 'First Frame Guided Editing'. Its first frame is marked 'Edited First Frame', and the hibiscus is replaced by a small red rose. The rose then grows across later frames while the rest of the scene is preserved. The bottom row is labeled 'Guided with Additional Edited Frame'. It uses the same first frame, but the last frame is marked 'Edited Additional Frame' and shows a large, fully bloomed red rose. Yellow boxes labeled 'Edited Region' and a zoomed inset of the stamen show that unedited regions are preserved. Curved black arrows run from the source's first and last frames to the edited rows. The eye goes first to the red roses against the teal background.
caption: Given a source video (top row), we achieve high-quality video editing guided by the first frame as a reference image (middle row), while maintaining flexibility for incorporating additional reference conditions (bottom row).
abstract: Video editing using diffusion models has achieved remarkable results in generating high-quality edits for videos. However, current methods often rely on large-scale pretraining, limiting flexibility for specific edits. First-frame-guided editing provides control over the first frame, but lacks fine-grained control over the edit's subsequent temporal evolution. To address this, we propose a mask-based LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) tuning method that adapts pretrained Image-to-Video models for flexible video editing. Our key innovation is using a spatiotemporal mask to strategically guide the LoRA fine-tuning process. This teaches the model two distinct skills: first, to interpret the mask as a command to either preserve content from the source video or generate new content in designated regions. Second, for these generated regions, LoRA learns to synthesize either temporally consistent motion inherited from the video or novel appearances guided by user-provided reference frames. This dual-capability LoRA grants users control over the edit's entire temporal evolution, allowing complex transformations like an object rotating or a flower blooming. Experimental results show our method achieves superior video editing performance compared to baseline methods. The code and video results are available at our project website: https://cjeen.github.io/LoRAEdit.
